title: Silence

segments.voice: Yesterday's word: menuchat hanefesh, calm of soul, the jar that clears when you set it down. Your line was calm soul. Did one breath come before one reply? Today, a new week, and a trait made of saying less. Day one thousand two hundred sixty-one.

The group chat has been going all morning. Opinions, jokes, a small argument, someone apologizing for the argument, someone else restarting it. Then one person who hasn't said anything all day types a single sentence, and everyone stops. Why does that one land? Partly because it's good. Partly because it came out of quiet. Words from someone who speaks all the time blur together. Words from someone who keeps silence get weighed. A sage in the Mishnah grew up among the sages, and came to a conclusion about this. It's today's word.
screen: `THE CHAT HASN'T STOPPED.` → `ONE SENTENCE FROM THE QUIET ONE.` → `WORDS FROM SILENCE GET WEIGHED.`

segments.voice: Shtikah. Silence. Four angles. First, the sage. In Pirkei Avot, Shimon, the son of Rabban Gamliel, says that all his days he grew up among the sages, and he found nothing better for the body than silence. Then he adds two more lines: what matters most is not study but doing, and whoever multiplies words brings on sin. He grew up surrounded by learned voices, and what he came away with was the value of the closed mouth. Second, Proverbs. The book of Proverbs says that even a fool, when he holds his peace, is counted wise, and one who shuts his lips is thought to have understanding. That's half a joke and half a warning: fewer words leave fewer chances to show what you don't know, and fewer chances to hurt someone. Third, the practice. Some Jews keep what's called a taanit dibbur, a fast from speech: a set stretch of hours with no talking at all, sometimes in a season of repentance. Some Mussar teachers recommend smaller versions, an hour, a meal, a commute, as a way of feeling how much of what we say is filler, or heat, or a reach to be seen. Fourth, the measure. Like every trait this block, silence has a right amount. Remember the two pockets from humility day: there are moments when staying quiet is a failure, when someone is being wronged or a truth needs saying. Shtikah isn't swallowing what matters. It's clearing away what doesn't, so that what matters can be heard. Words that come out of quiet can be fewer, kinder and more true.
screen: `NOTHING BETTER THAN SILENCE.` · `EVEN A FOOL IS COUNTED WISE.` · `A FAST FROM SPEECH.` · `NOT SWALLOWING WHAT MATTERS.` · then, large: `SILENCE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: keep silent for an hour. Start now, with the two minutes the bell holds. Settle, and breathe. Close your mouth gently; let your tongue rest. Notice the words that still rise: things to say, replies to rehearse, a comment for later. You don't have to stop them. Just watch them come and go, unspoken. Then choose your hour for later today. A commute, a walk, a stretch of chores, an hour with the phone face down. If someone needs you, answer them; this is a practice, not a wall. If you pray, you can let the silence itself be a kind of listening. If you don't, simply let it be quiet. The bell holds the time.
Shtikah. Silence: guarding speech by speaking less, so the words that do come out are worth weighing. Today's word.
Your line: silence. Today, keep one hour of quiet, and afterward notice which of the words you held back still seem worth saying. Day one thousand two hundred sixty-one.

howItsDone: Some Jews keep a taanit dibbur, a set stretch of time with no speech, and in Mussar practice people working on shtikah set themselves shorter periods of silence, such as an hour or a meal.

what a scholar hears: Avot's sage, raised among the sages, finding nothing better than silence, and pairing it with doing over study.

notes: Avot 1:17 paraphrased (Shimon son of Rabban Gamliel: nothing better for the body/person than silence; not study but deed is the essential thing; one who multiplies words brings sin). The Mishnah says 'for the body'; the lesson says 'for a person'. Confirm.
'He had spent his life around learned talkers' expands 'grew up among the sages'; trim if too strong.
Taanit dibbur described as kept by 'some Jews', 'sometimes in a season of repentance'; confirm.
Akiva's 'silence is a fence for wisdom' (Avot 3:13) left out because y4 day 1145 uses it; Ecclesiastes 3:7 left out because y3 day 854 uses it.
